primer.intro: Before trees and graphs there are loops, remainders and the discipline of checking your own work. This topic is the gym for that discipline. Its problems look tiny - count the digits of a number, reverse it, test it for primality, add up an array - but each one trains a move that every later topic assumes you own: peeling a number apart with modulo and division, carrying an accumulator through a loop, guarding the edge values, and dry-running four lines of code on paper until the trace and the program agree. Nothing here needs a data structure beyond an array. Everything here decides how fast the harder topics will go.
whenToUse: Taking a number apart digit by digit: remainder 10 reads the last digit, division by 10 drops it.
Building a number from digits: multiply the accumulator by 10 and add - reversal is this one line.
Testing divisibility properties: trial division needs to climb only to the square root.
GCD questions: Euclid's remainder dance beats any factor list.
Summaries over an array - sum, count, largest - are one accumulator and one pass.
primer.mentalModel: Every number is a queue of digits that modulo and division let you pop from the right. The loop while n is positive: take n remainder 10, then divide n by 10 - reads the digits last-to-first, and almost every digit problem is that loop plus a different line in the middle: count one per pass, push onto a growing reverse, track a maximum, add into a sum. The second standing idea is the paired divisor: when d divides n, so does n over d, and one of the pair sits at or below the square root - so primality needs only square-root many checks. The third is Euclid: the gcd of a and b equals the gcd of b and a remainder b, which shrinks fast enough to finish in a handful of steps. Three small ideas, endlessly recombined.
mistakes: Destroying the input while computing - reverse eats n, then the palindrome compare runs against the eaten value; keep a copy.
Forgetting the edges below 2: a while-positive digit loop counts zero digits for 0, and 1 is no prime.
Looping to n instead of its square root in primality tests - correct, but a million times slower near a billion.

example.title: Reversing a number with the digit loop
example.explain: Each pass pops the last digit of n and pushes it onto rev from the right - rev times 10 slides the digits already collected one place left to make room. Trace it on 1200: rev walks 0, 2, 21 as the zeros melt into the multiplication, which is why the reverse of 1200 is 21 and no leading-zero bookkeeping is ever needed. The same skeleton counts digits, sums them or finds the largest - only the middle line changes.

primer.practice: Open Practice with Count All Digits, then do Reverse a Number immediately after - the second is the first with one line swapped, and feeling that is the lesson.

sections.title: The digit loop
sections.text: One loop underlies half this topic: while n is positive, read n remainder 10, then divide n by 10 (integer division). The remainder is the rightmost digit; the division shifts the whole number one place right. Counting passes counts digits. Adding remainders sums digits. Comparing each remainder to a running maximum finds the largest digit. Feeding remainders into rev times 10 plus digit builds the reversal. Two edges deserve respect: 0 makes the while-positive loop run zero times, so a digit counter must special-case it or use a do-while; and any compare-against-the-original trick - palindromes, Armstrong numbers - must stash a copy first, because the loop grinds n down to 0 as a side effect.

check.prompt: Run rev = rev * 10 + n % 10 with n = n div 10 each pass, starting rev at 0. What does n = 1200 produce?

options.explain: Passes build 0, 2, 21 - the trailing zeros of 1200 vanish into the multiply.
Numbers carry no leading zeros; the value is just 21.
That keeps the digits in place - reversal reads them from the right.
12 would be the front half; the loop reads from the back.

reveal.solution: Trace it. n=1200: digit 0, rev = 0. n=120: digit 0, rev = 0. n=12: digit 2, rev = 2. n=1: digit 1, rev = 21. n=0 stops the loop. The reverse of 1200 is 21 - leading zeros of the reversal simply never exist, because rev is a number, and multiplying 0 by 10 keeps it 0. No string padding, no special cases.

sections.title: Pairs, halves and remainders
sections.text: Divisors arrive in pairs: when d divides n, its partner n over d divides n too, and the smaller of each pair is at most the square root of n. So a primality test climbs only to the square root - near a billion that is about thirty-one thousand checks instead of a billion - and a divisor lister collects both partners per hit. Euclid's algorithm runs on the same remainder operator from the digit loop: gcd(a, b) equals gcd(b, a mod b), repeated until the second number is 0, and the first is the answer. It shrinks at least geometrically, finishing in dozens of steps where factor-listing would wander. The lcm follows free of charge: a times b divided by their gcd - divide before multiplying to dodge overflow.

quiz.prompt: Count the digits of a positive integer with arithmetic only. The loop?

options.text: While n stays positive: divide n by 10 and count one pass per digit
options.explain: Each division drops one digit; the pass count is the digit count.

options.text: Multiply n by 10 until it overflows
options.explain: Growing the number says nothing about how many digits it started with.
Subtraction counts tens, one digit's worth - division shifts whole places.

options.text: Add the digits and read the total
options.explain: A digit sum measures value, the count measures length.

quiz.prompt: Reverse the digits of a number inside the digit loop. The middle line?

options.text: rev = rev * 10 + (n % 10) - slide left, append the popped digit
options.explain: The multiply makes room on the right; the remainder fills it.
Plain adding sums the digits instead of positioning them.
Dividing rev erases what was already built.
That shifts n itself, collecting nothing across passes.

quiz.prompt: Test whether n is prime by trial division. How far must the loop climb?

options.text: To the square root - divisors pair up across it
options.explain: A divisor above the root has a partner below it, already checked.
Correct but wasteful - a billion checks where thirty thousand suffice.
Half of n is still vastly beyond the square root.
Composites like 1009 times 1013 pass any fixed-size check list.

quiz.prompt: Compute gcd(a, b) quickly, with no factor lists. The method?

options.text: Euclid: keep replacing the pair (a, b) by (b, a mod b) until b is 0
options.explain: The remainder shrinks fast; the surviving value is the gcd.

options.text: List both numbers' divisors and intersect
options.explain: Works, but costs square-root scans and set bookkeeping Euclid skips.

options.text: Divide the larger by the smaller and round
options.explain: A quotient is a ratio - the gcd is about shared structure.

options.text: Multiply them and halve until odd
options.explain: That computes nothing related; halving ruins odd factors.

quiz.prompt: What is the reverse of 1200 as a number?

options.explain: The trailing zeros dissolve - rev walks 0, 0, 2, 21.
2100 keeps the digits in their old places.
12 reads the front of the number; the loop reads the back.
Only palindromes survive reversal unchanged.

quiz.prompt: Euclid on gcd(12, 18): list the pairs until the second entry hits 0.

options.explain: Each step takes the remainder; 6 survives when the partner dies.
Halving both numbers is no step of Euclid; remainders drive it.
12 mod 6 is 0, but the pair swaps first: gcd(6, 0) ends it at 6.
Adding the numbers grows them; the gcd can be no bigger than either.

quiz.prompt: Feed 5678 through the divide-by-10 loop. How many passes before n reaches 0?

options.explain: 5678, 567, 56, 5, 0 - one pass per digit.
The final 5 still needs a pass to become 0.
Division by 10 jumps a whole place, no counting by ones.
Ten is the base, the passes follow the digit count.

quiz.prompt: How many passes does the digit loop make on a number n?

options.text: About log base 10 of n - one per digit
options.explain: A 9-digit number takes 9 passes; growth is logarithmic in the value.
Linear in the value would be a billion passes for a billion.
The base is 10; the pass count tracks the number's length.
The root belongs to divisor pairing, a different trick.

quiz.prompt: Trial division to the square root, n near one billion - roughly how many checks?

options.explain: The square root of a billion is about 31623 - instant on any machine.
That is the cost of looping to n itself, the thing the root avoids.
Thirty is the digit-loop scale; primality pays the square root.
A million squared is a trillion - overshoots n by a factor of a thousand.

quiz.prompt: This palindrome check says no to every number, even 121. What is the bug?

options.text: The loop grinds n to 0, then compares rev against that 0 - stash a copy first
options.explain: Compare rev to the saved original; the loop's n is a casualty.
Starting at 1 plants a phantom digit in every reversal.

options.text: The modulo and division are swapped
options.explain: Read the digit before dropping it - the order shown is right.
Without it, fractional n poisons the next remainder.

quiz.prompt: isPrime(1) returns true from this code. What is the bug?

options.text: Values below 2 skip the loop entirely and fall through to true - guard n less than 2
options.explain: For n = 1 the loop body runs zero times; the guard must be explicit.
Starting at 1 declares everything composite - 1 divides all.
At these sizes the square is safe; the missing guard is the flaw.

options.text: return true and false are swapped
options.explain: Finding a divisor rightly means composite.

quiz.prompt: Which input most deserves a dedicated test for a digit counter?

options.text: 0 - the while-positive loop runs zero times and reports zero digits
options.explain: Zero has one digit; a special case or do-while is required.
Big but regular - the loop handles it like any other.
The last digit's value changes nothing about counting.
Binary structure is invisible to a base-10 loop.
